summary: Jesus rebukes the towns that saw His mighty works and did not repent, thanks the Father for revealing these things to babes, and calls the weary to His rest.
key_insight: Jesus’ gentlest invitation comes right after woes on the towns He knew best and His highest claim: “All things have been delivered to Me by My Father.” The One who holds all things then describes His own heart, the only time in the Gospels He does so: “gentle and lowly.”
story: Then Jesus began to rebuke the cities in which most of His mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” If the mighty works done in them had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities “would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” It would be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for them.

Then He turned to Capernaum, the town where He had made His home: “And you, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades.” If Sodom had seen the mighty works done there, “it would have remained until this day.” Even the land of Sodom would fare better in the day of judgment.

At that time Jesus answered and said, “I thank You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to babes.” He gladly accepted the Father’s way: “Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in Your sight.”

“All things have been delivered to Me by My Father,” He said, “and no one knows the Son except the Father.” Nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.

Then He gave the invitation: “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”

fit.question: Luke records the woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, and the prayer thanking the Father for revealing these things to babes, in a different setting: when Jesus sent out the Seventy and when they returned (Luke 10:13–15, 21–22). When did Jesus say these words?

points.label: Spoken more than once
points.text: A teacher who travels from town to town repeats his weightiest sayings. Luke ties the prayer closely to the Seventy’s return (“In that hour,” 10:21), and his wording differs slightly from Matthew’s. Only Matthew records the invitation to the weary that follows.

points.label: Matthew groups by theme
points.text: Matthew often gathers Jesus’ teaching by subject, as in the Sermon on the Mount and the parables of chapter 13, and his “Then” and “At that time” (11:20, 25) can join sayings loosely. Edersheim thought Luke gives the original setting and Matthew placed the words here, beside the people’s rejection of John and of Jesus.

fit.note: Whether Jesus spoke these words twice or Matthew set them beside related teaching, both writers report what Jesus truly said.
fit.short: Jesus may have spoken these words on two occasions, or Matthew grouped them with related teaching; only Matthew records the invitation itself.

scene.label: Capernaum, His own city
scene.text: Jesus had left Nazareth and made His home in Capernaum (Matthew 4:13; 9:1), and many of the miracles the Gospels record happened there. His words echo Isaiah’s taunt against the proud king of Babylon, who said, “I will ascend into heaven,” and was told, “Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol” (Isaiah 14:13, 15).

scene.label: Sodom
scene.text: Sodom was Scripture’s byword for wickedness and sudden judgment; the LORD rained fire and brimstone on it (Genesis 19:24). Abraham had pleaded for the city, and God promised to spare it for the sake of ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32). Jesus says that if it had seen what Capernaum saw, it would still be standing.

scene.label: The wise and the babes
scene.text: Isaiah had warned that “the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, And the understanding of their prudent men shall be hidden” (Isaiah 29:14). In Jesus’ day the learned were the scribes and teachers trained in the Law. Many who received Him had no such training: fishermen, a tax collector, and the crowd the Pharisees dismissed as one “that does not know the law” (John 7:49).

scene.label: A yoke
scene.text: A yoke was a wooden beam fitted across the necks of working animals. Jewish teachers spoke of the Law as a yoke a faithful Israelite took upon himself, and later rabbinic writings speak of taking on the yoke of the kingdom of heaven. Peter would later warn against laying on believers “a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear” (Acts 15:10).

scene.label: Rest for your souls
scene.text: Jesus’ promise repeats Jeremiah 6:16, where the LORD told Israel to ask for the old paths and walk in the good way: “Then you will find rest for your souls.” Israel answered, “We will not walk in it.” Jesus now says that this rest is found by coming to Him.

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew records the invitation to the weary. He sets it right after the woes on the unrepentant towns and just before two Sabbath disputes (12:1–14), so the promise of rest stands beside the Pharisees’ quarrels over the day of rest. Later Matthew calls the King “lowly” as He rides into Jerusalem (21:5), and records Jesus’ charge that the scribes “bind heavy burdens, hard to bear” (23:4).

seeing.reveals: Jesus claims what no prophet ever claimed: all things are in His hands, and only He can make the Father known. Yet the same Lord calls Himself gentle and lowly in heart and invites everyone who is worn out and weighed down to come to Him.
seeing.living: Jesus does not promise rest by removing every yoke; He offers His own and says, “learn from Me.” Capernaum saw His works and stayed where it was; this invitation is answered only by coming. Bring Him the load you carry, including the demands He never laid on you, and take up the yoke of a Teacher who is gentle with His learners.
seeing.ponder: Do you think of Jesus as gentle and lowly in heart toward you, and if not, what has taught you otherwise?

preaching.big_idea: The Son who alone knows the Father invites the weary to His easy yoke.
outline: Woe to those who saw and would not repent (20–24)
Revealed to babes by the Father’s will (25–26)
Rest under the gentle Teacher’s yoke (28–30)
preaching.watch_for: The word “all” joins the claim to the call: “All things have been delivered to Me” (v. 27) and “Come to Me, all you who labor” (v. 28). Matthew follows the promise of rest at once with two Sabbath disputes, introduced with the same “At that time” (12:1).
